title: Uddhava Praises the Gopis and Departs
story:
Uddhava had come to Vrindavan expecting to console. Krishna's own friend and counsellor, sent from Mathura with a message for the gopis — the cowherd women who had loved Krishna since his boyhood in the village — he had thought he would find grief and leave comfort. Instead the learned man stood humbled, and the wish that rose in him was one no teacher was supposed to make. He had listened to the gopis answer Krishna's message, and what he had seen in them rearranged everything he thought he knew about worth.

He did not leave at once. He stayed some months in Vrindavan, easing the sorrow of the women who had become his teachers. Day by day he walked the country, looking at the rivers, the forests, the valleys, and the flowering trees, and day by day he watched the gopis in their state — wholly absorbed in Krishna, their minds carried away by him, so agitated with love that the place itself seemed to shake with their longing. And as he watched, the praise poured out of him. Wherever he looked — a river bend, a stand of trees, a hill in the distance — he saw how thoroughly the place and its people belonged to Krishna, and how thoroughly Krishna belonged to them.

These cowherd women, he said, have reached the highest place any living being can reach. Their hearts are fixed on Krishna, the soul of all things; what good is even a brahmana birth, he asked — the priestly birth that the whole world honours — compared to the taste of the endless stories about him? Consider the distance between the two — where are these simple forest women, and where is the soul of all things? — and yet he has made them his own. The embrace that even the gods long for was given to these women of Vrindavan at the rasa dance, the night-dance of the forest. This blessing, he said, has not been granted even to the goddess of fortune herself, nor to the lotus-scented women of heaven; how then could anyone lesser hope for it? And the Lord bestows his highest good even on the ignorant who serve him, the way the best of medicines heals one who takes it without understanding what it is. These women had thrown away their families and the straight road of duty for the path that the scriptures themselves search for.

And then the wish that turned the whole order upside down. May I become any shrub, any creeper, any herb at all in Vrindavan, blessed by the dust of these gopis' feet. Again and again he bowed to that dust — I bow to the foot-dust of the women of Nanda's village, again and again — the man of learning wanting nothing more than to grow from the roadside where they walked.

When the time came to go, he had one more duty. He comforted Nanda and Yashoda — the cowherd chief and his wife who had raised Krishna — and the cowherds, speaking to them of Krishna, and they honored him as they would a brother, coming to him with offerings in their hands. Their one wish, spoken plainly, was that their minds might rest forever at Krishna's lotus feet, wherever the wandering of their lives might take them. Uddhava bowed toward Krishna, wherever he was, and set out on the road back to Mathura, carrying the news of how the people of Vrindavan loved him still — a devotion he could now measure, because he had felt a share of it himself. When he reached Mathura he told Krishna plainly of the fullness of the devotion he had found among the cowherds.

He had gone to console, and had been the one changed. A counsellor of kings had asked to be a roadside shrub, and no one who heard him thought the wish foolish.
reflection: Uddhava's wish to become a shrub in Vrindavan quietly reverses every ranking he brought with him. The man of learning envies not the gopis' knowledge but their totality — they gave away everything the world calls secure and gained the one thing the scriptures point toward but cannot hand over.
next_story_tease: Not long after Uddhava returned to Mathura, another envoy set out for Vrindavan — a man named Akrura, sent by the king.
hero_scene: Uddhava bowing low before the gopis in a flowering Vrindavan grove, his head lowered to the dust of their feet, the learned man praying to become a shrub or creeper growing from the roadside.
